evidence.cards.0.title.source: Three posts about Hillside Learning Centre
evidence.cards.0.title.back: Three posts about Hillside Learning Centre

evidence.cards.0.cases.0.body.source: “CENTRE CLOSED FOREVER TOMORROW!!! Share now.” There is no name, no date and no link.
evidence.cards.0.cases.0.body.back: "The centre is closed forever from tomorrow. Share now." No name, no date and no link.
evidence.cards.0.cases.0.body.note: The English post shouts with capital letters and '!!!'. Thai has no capital letters and the brief forbids exclamation marks, so the Thai post is plain (ศูนย์ปิดถาวรตั้งแต่พรุ่งนี้ แชร์เลยตอนนี้) and the reading speaks of ตัวหนังสือตัวใหญ่ (big letters). Check whether the urgency still comes through; the picture shows ด่วนมาก / ปิดถาวร / แชร์เลย.

evidence.cards.0.cases.1.body.source: A notice on the centre's own page, signed by the centre manager and dated today: “The centre will be closed on Tuesday from 9 to 12 for water pipe repairs. We open again at 12 noon.”
evidence.cards.0.cases.1.body.back: A notice on the centre's own page, signed by the centre manager and dated today: "The centre will close on Tuesday from 9 to 12 o'clock to repair a water pipe. We will open again at noon, 12 o'clock."
evidence.cards.0.cases.1.body.note: Times '9 to 12' and '12 noon' written ตั้งแต่ 9 ถึง 12 นาฬิกา and เที่ยงวัน 12 นาฬิกา, without the abbreviation น. (the text is read aloud). Check this sounds natural; Thai might say 9 โมงเช้าถึงเที่ยง.

evidence.cards.0.cases.2.body.source: A photo of the centre's locked door, sent by a neighbour. The date on the photo shows it was taken last year.
evidence.cards.0.cases.2.body.back: A photo of the centre's locked door, sent by a neighbour. The date on the photo shows it was taken last year.

evidence.cards.1.cases.0.body.source: “Free football boots for every child at City Park on Saturday. Forward this to 10 friends.” It does not say who is giving the boots.
evidence.cards.1.cases.0.body.back: "Free football boots for every child at City Park this Saturday. Forward this message to 10 friends." The message doesn't say who is giving out the boots.
evidence.cards.1.cases.0.body.note: City Park and Lakeside are invented place names, kept in Latin letters.

evidence.cards.1.cases.1.body.source: “Sleeping next to a cut onion stops all colds. Doctors don't want you to know.” No doctor or health organisation is named.
evidence.cards.1.cases.1.body.back: "Sleeping next to a cut onion stops every kind of cold. Doctors don't want you to know." No doctor or health organisation is named.
evidence.cards.1.cases.1.body.note: 'stops all colds' is ช่วยหยุดหวัดได้ทุกชนิด. 'health organisation' องค์กรด้านสุขภาพ; 'health worker' (reading) เจ้าหน้าที่สาธารณสุข.

evidence.cards.1.cases.2.body.source: A photo of a fish as long as a bus, “caught at Lakeside yesterday”. The edges of the fish look strange, and nobody else has a photo of it.
evidence.cards.1.cases.2.body.back: A picture of a fish as long as a bus, "caught at Lakeside yesterday". The edges of the fish look strange, and no one else has this picture at all.

read.sections.0.heading.source: Loud is not the same as true

read.sections.0.text.source: Messages spread very fast on phones and messaging apps. Some are true, some are honest mistakes and some are completely invented. A message with capital letters that says “Share now” can feel urgent, but that does not make it true. To judge any claim, first identify its source. Post A has no name, no date and no link, so nobody can tell where it really came from. Post B is a signed notice on the centre's own page, and it is dated today. It also gives evidence: exact times and a clear reason for the closure. A clear source with specific details is usually more trustworthy.
read.sections.0.text.back: Messages spread very fast by phone and messaging apps. Some messages are true, some are mistakes made without meaning to, and some are completely made up. A message written in big letters that says "Share now" may make you feel it is urgent, but that doesn't make it true. To judge any claim, first look for its source. Post A has no name, no date and no link, so no one can know where it really came from. Post B is a signed notice on the centre's own page, dated today. It also has evidence: an exact time and a clear reason for closing. Clear sources with specific details are usually more trustworthy.
read.sections.0.text.note: Lesson 23 (judging information): translated closely, no idea added or removed. 'capital letters' is ตัวหนังสือตัวใหญ่. source = แหล่งข้อมูล, claim = คำกล่าวอ้าง (KEY_TERMS, check), evidence = หลักฐาน. 'Share now' is แชร์เลยตอนนี้ everywhere.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Messages move fast on phones. Some are true. Some are wrong. A post in big letters that says “Share now” can feel important. But that does not make it true. When you see a claim, ask about the source. Who made it? Post A has no name and no date. Post B comes from the centre itself. It has a date. It also has evidence, like exact times. So Post B is easier to trust.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Messages spread fast by phone. Some messages are true. Some are not true. A post written in big letters saying "Share now" may seem important, but that doesn't make it true. When you see a claim, ask about the source. Who made it? Post A has no name and no date. Post B comes from the centre itself, has a date and also has evidence, such as an exact time. So Post B is more trustworthy.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Check the date and the context

read.sections.1.text.source: Even a real photo can mislead people. Post C shows a real locked door, but the photo is from last year, so it cannot tell us anything about tomorrow. The date, the place and the reason for a photo are its context, and context changes what a photo means. Photos can also be edited with apps, or even made by a computer. The giant fish in Message F looks strange at the edges, and nobody else has a picture of it. When a photo or story seems surprising, look for the same news from another trusted source.
read.sections.1.text.back: Even a real photo can mislead people. Post C shows a door that really is locked, but the photo was taken last year, so it tells us nothing at all about tomorrow. A photo's date, place and reason are its context, and context changes what a photo means. Photos can also be edited with apps, or even created by computers. The giant fish in Message F looks strange at the edges, and no one else has a picture of it at all. When a photo or story seems surprising, look for the same news from other trustworthy sources.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: A real photo can still trick you. Post C shows a real door. But the photo is from last year. It does not show tomorrow. When and where a photo was taken is its context. Context can change what a photo means. Some photos are changed with apps. Some are made by computers. The big fish in Message F looks strange. No one else has a photo of it. Look for the news in another place you trust.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: A real photo can still trick you. Post C shows a real door, but the photo was taken last year. This photo doesn't tell about tomorrow. When and where a photo was taken is its context. Context can change what a photo means. Some photos are edited with apps. Some are made by computers. The big fish in Message F looks strange. No one else has a picture of it. Try finding this news somewhere else you trust.

read.sections.2.text.source: A rumour is a story that spreads from person to person without proof. Message D and Message E are both like rumours. Message D does not explain who is giving away the free boots. Message E says “doctors don't want you to know”, but it names no doctor or health organisation. Before sharing any message, try to verify it. Ask three questions: Who made it? When was it made? What is the evidence? Then compare it with a trusted source, such as a teacher, a health worker or an official notice. If you cannot verify a message, it is usually safer not to forward it.
read.sections.2.text.back: A rumour is a story that spreads from one person to another without evidence to confirm it. Message D and Message E are both like rumours. Message D doesn't explain who is giving out the free boots. Message E says "Doctors don't want you to know" but doesn't name any doctor or health organisation at all. Before sharing any message, try checking it first. Ask three questions: Who made it? When was it made? What is the evidence? Then compare with trustworthy sources, such as a teacher, a health worker or an official notice. If you can't verify a message, not forwarding it is usually safer.
read.sections.2.text.note: The three questions keep question marks: ใครเป็นคนทำ? ทำขึ้นเมื่อไร? หลักฐานคืออะไร? 'official notice' ประกาศอย่างเป็นทางการ.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: A rumour is a story that spreads with no proof. Messages D and E are like rumours. They do not say who made them. Before you share, try to verify the message. Ask: Who made it? When? What is the evidence? Then ask someone you trust, like a teacher or a health worker. If you cannot check it, do not send it on.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: A rumour is a story that spreads without evidence. Messages D and E are like rumours. Neither says who made it. Before sharing, try checking the message first. Ask: Who made it? When? What is the evidence? Then ask someone you trust, such as a teacher or a health worker. If you can't verify it, don't forward it.

watch.why.source: It explains how facts, opinions and mistakes get into the news, and how a careful reader can tell them apart.

watch.beforeQuestion.source: What makes you trust a piece of news?
watch.beforeQuestion.back: What makes you believe a news story?

watch.afterQuestion.source: Why can a true photo or a true fact still mislead people?
watch.afterQuestion.back: Why can a real photo or a correct fact still mislead people?

watch.summary.source: This animated video is about how to choose your news. Not long ago, most people got news from a few newspapers and TV channels. Now the internet brings much more news, from many more people. Different sources may even disagree about the facts. The video gives some tips. When you can, find the first source, like the real report or speech. When a big story is still happening, do not check every few minutes. Wait for clear facts. Read the same story in more than one place. Look for words like “think”, “likely” or “probably”. They show that a report is not sure. Be careful when a report does not say who gave the facts. Most important, check a story before you share it.
watch.summary.back: This animated video is about how to choose your news. Not long ago, most people got news from newspapers and a few TV channels. Now the internet brings much more news, from many more people. Different sources may disagree, even about facts. The video gives some advice. If you can, find the first source, such as the actual report or speech. When a big story is still happening, don't check every few minutes; wait for clear facts. Read the same news from more than one place. Notice words like "think", "probably" or "might": these show the report isn't sure yet. Be careful when a report doesn't say who gave the facts. Most important, check news before sharing.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: The examples are everyday and neutral on purpose: a centre closure, free boots, a health myth and an edited photo. Do not use real rumours about sensitive topics, such as legal processes, aid or official services, in class. If a learner raises one, do not debate the details; point them to the official organisation that runs that service.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: The lesson's examples are deliberately everyday and neutral: a centre closing, free shoes, a false health belief and an edited photo. Don't use real rumours about sensitive topics in class, such as legal processes, aid or official services. If a learner mentions a rumour like that, don't debate the details; suggest they ask the official organisation responsible for that service.
sensitiveNotes.0.note: 'aid or official services' is ความช่วยเหลือ หรือบริการของทางการ. Check the register for adults and that 'legal processes' (กระบวนการทางกฎหมาย) is understood broadly.

educatorNotes.0.back: Make clear that the onion tip in Message E is a false belief. For health questions, learners should ask a health worker or a clinic.
